claim: E2 stimulation causes a rapid, global increase in the formation of R-loops in ER-positive breast epithelial cells.
source: Here, we show that E2 stimulation causes a rapid, global increase in the formation of R-loops, co-transcriptional RNA-DNA products, which in some instances have been linked to DNA damage.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: E2-dependent R-loop formation is highly enriched at E2-responsive genomic loci.
source: We show that E2-dependent R-loop formation and breast cancer rearrangements are highly enriched at E2-responsive genomic loci and that E2 induces DNA replication-dependent double-strand breaks (DSBs).
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by DRIP-seq data and GREAT analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: E2 induces DNA replication-dependent double-strand breaks (DSBs).
source: We show that E2-dependent R-loop formation and breast cancer rearrangements are highly enriched at E2-responsive genomic loci and that E2 induces DNA replication-dependent double-strand breaks (DSBs).
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by EdU staining and Cdc7 inhibitor experiments shown in Figure 1F-H.

claim: Many DSBs that accumulate in response to E2 are R-loop dependent.
source: Strikingly, many DSBs that accumulate in response to E2 are R-loop dependent.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by RNase H overexpression experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Higher E2 serum concentrations are positively correlated with an increased incidence of sporadic breast cancer.
source: Specifically, higher E2 serum concentrations and longer lifetime E2 exposure are both positively correlated with an increased incidence of sporadic breast cancer (Clemons and Goss, 2001; Colditz, 1998; Hilakivi-Clarke et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Longer lifetime E2 exposure is positively correlated with an increased incidence of sporadic breast cancer.
source: Specifically, higher E2 serum concentrations and longer lifetime E2 exposure are both positively correlated with an increased incidence of sporadic breast cancer (Clemons and Goss, 2001; Colditz, 1998; Hilakivi-Clarke et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: E2 leads to DNA damage in breast epithelial cells that express the estrogen receptor (ER).
source: Moreover, E2 leads to DNA damage in breast epithelial cells that express the estrogen receptor (ER) (Liehr, 2000; Williamson and Lees-Miller, 2011), and in rat models, E2 stimulation is causally linked to chromosome instability and aneuploidy (Li et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In rat models, E2 stimulation is causally linked to chromosome instability and aneuploidy.
source: Moreover, E2 leads to DNA damage in breast epithelial cells that express the estrogen receptor (ER) (Liehr, 2000; Williamson and Lees-Miller, 2011), and in rat models, E2 stimulation is causally linked to chromosome instability and aneuploidy (Li et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: E2 governs the expression of thousands of genes in breast cells through its association with the nuclear hormone receptors ER-α and ER-β.
source: Functionally, E2 is a key transcriptional regulator that governs the expression of thousands of genes in breast cells (Cheung and Kraus, 2010; Hah et al., 2011) through its association with the nuclear hormone receptors ER-α and ER-β.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The E2-ER complex binds to estrogen-response elements or to other transcription factors, thus altering gene expression.
source: Upon translocation into the nucleus, the E2-ER complex binds to estrogen-response elements or to other transcription factors, thus altering gene expression (Marino et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: R-loops are proposed to serve regulatory roles in the cell including the patterning of promoter chromatin and the facilitation of transcription termination.
source: These structures are proposed to serve regulatory roles in the cell including the patterning of promoter chromatin and the facilitation of transcription termination (Ginno et al., 2012; Skourti-Stathaki et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The coordinated cleavage of an R-loop at the switch region in B-cells facilitates recombination and generates antibody diversity.
source: The coordinated cleavage of an R-loop at the switch region in B-cells facilitates recombination and generates antibody diversity (Santos-Pereira and Aguilera, 2015; Yu et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The loss of RNA processing and R-loop regulatory factors results in an increase in R-loops and R-loop-dependent DNA damage in both yeast and human cells.
source: For example, the loss of RNA processing and R-loop regulatory factors results in an increase in R-loops and R-loop-dependent DNA damage in both yeast and human cells (Garcia-Rubio et al., 2015; Huertas and Aguilera, 2003; Li and Manley, 2005; Paulsen et al., 2009; Sollier et al., 2014; Tuduri et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: R-loops are enriched at rDNA repeats.
source: This is evidenced by the enrichment of R-loops at rDNA repeats (El Hage et al., 2010) and the binding of the R-loop suppressing factor Npl3 preferentially at the most highly transcribed genes (Santos-Pereira et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The R-loop suppressing factor Npl3 binds preferentially at the most highly transcribed genes.
source: This is evidenced by the enrichment of R-loops at rDNA repeats (El Hage et al., 2010) and the binding of the R-loop suppressing factor Npl3 preferentially at the most highly transcribed genes (Santos-Pereira et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: E2 treatment leads to a dose-dependent increase in P-H2AX intensity 24 hr after E2 addition in MCF7 cells.
source: We observed a clear, dose-dependent increase in P-H2AX intensity 24 hr after E2 addition (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: E2 treatment results in an increase in 53BP1 foci in MCF7 cells.
source: E2 treatment also resulted in an increase in 53BP1 foci (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), another marker of damaged DNA.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cells treated with 1 or 100 nM E2 had similar cell cycle profiles despite significantly different P-H2AX levels.
source: Notably, cells treated with 1 or 100 nM E2 had similar cell cycle profiles (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), despite significantly different P-H2AX levels, suggesting that the increase in DNA damage was not due to differences in the S phase population.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by FACS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The increase in DNA damage following E2 treatment was not due to differences in the S phase population.
source: Notably, cells treated with 1 or 100 nM E2 had similar cell cycle profiles (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), despite significantly different P-H2AX levels, suggesting that the increase in DNA damage was not due to differences in the S phase population.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that cells with similar cell cycle profiles had different P-H2AX levels.

claim: ER-negative MCF10A breast epithelial cells showed no significant change in P-H2AX signal when treated with 100 nM E2.
source: Importantly, ER-negative MCF10A breast epithelial cells showed no significant change in P-H2AX signal when treated with 100 nM E2 (Figure 1—figure supplements 3A,B), consistent with the previous finding that E2-induced DNA damage depends on the ER (Williamson and Lees-Miller, 2011).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 3A,B.

claim: E2-induced DNA damage depends on the ER.
source: Importantly, ER-negative MCF10A breast epithelial cells showed no significant change in P-H2AX signal when treated with 100 nM E2 (Figure 1—figure supplements 3A,B), consistent with the previous finding that E2-induced DNA damage depends on the ER (Williamson and Lees-Miller, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature and by the experimental data showing no P-H2AX increase in ER-negative cells.

claim: E2 treatment leads to an increase in DSBs as measured by the neutral comet assay.
source: The neutral comet assay provided direct evidence that E2 leads to DSB formation (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by neutral comet assay data shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: The P-H2AX signal resulting from 24 hr of E2 stimulation was significantly greater than the signal resulting from very short (10–40 min) treatments.
source: When we examined this early response to E2, we found that the P-H2AX signal resulting from 24 hr of E2 stimulation was significantly greater than the signal resulting from very short (10–40 min) treatments, raising the possibility that the later DNA breaks arise through a different mechanism (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by time-course data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The later DNA breaks arising from E2 treatment may arise through a different mechanism than the early breaks.
source: When we examined this early response to E2, we found that the P-H2AX signal resulting from 24 hr of E2 stimulation was significantly greater than the signal resulting from very short (10–40 min) treatments, raising the possibility that the later DNA breaks arise through a different mechanism (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observation of different kinetics of P-H2AX signal.

claim: The percentage of P-H2AX positive cells increased dramatically after 16 and 24 hr of E2 treatment, and the majority of these cells were EdU positive.
source: The percentage of P-H2AX positive cells increased dramatically after 16 and 24 hr, and the majority of these cells were EdU positive (Figure 1 F,G, and Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by EdU and P-H2AX co-staining data shown in Figure 1F,G.

claim: E2-induced DNA damage may require DNA replication.
source: This finding strongly suggests that E2-induced DNA damage may require DNA replication.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that P-H2AX positive cells are predominantly EdU positive.

claim: Treatment with a Cdc7 inhibitor (PHA 767491) that largely blocks S phase entry reduced E2-induced DNA damage.
source: Indeed, when we treated E2-stimulated cells with a Cdc7 inhibitor (PHA 767491) that largely blocks S phase entry (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A), we found that the DNA damage was reduced (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by P-H2AX quantification data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: At the 1 μM dose of PHA 767491 used, phosphorylation of RNA Pol II at Ser2 by Cdk9 was not inhibited.
source: At the 1 μM dose of PHA 767491 used, phosphorylation of RNA Pol II at Ser2 by Cdk9 was not inhibited, indicating the effect on P-H2AX is not a result of inhibiting RNA Pol II elongation (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5B.

claim: The effect of PHA 767491 on P-H2AX is not a result of inhibiting RNA Pol II elongation.
source: At the 1 μM dose of PHA 767491 used, phosphorylation of RNA Pol II at Ser2 by Cdk9 was not inhibited, indicating the effect on P-H2AX is not a result of inhibiting RNA Pol II elongation (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that RNA Pol II phosphorylation was not affected by the inhibitor.

claim: Treatment with the transcription inhibitor flavopiridol abolished the late E2-induced increase in P-H2AX.
source: Treatment with the transcription inhibitor flavopiridol abolished the late E2-induced increase in P-H2AX (Figure 1I) but did not significantly affect the percentage of cells in S phase (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by P-H2AX quantification data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Flavopiridol treatment did not significantly affect the percentage of cells in S phase.
source: Treatment with the transcription inhibitor flavopiridol abolished the late E2-induced increase in P-H2AX (Figure 1I) but did not significantly affect the percentage of cells in S phase (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by EdU staining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: E2 induces DSBs in a replication- and transcription-dependent manner.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that E2 induces DSBs in a replication- and transcription-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the experiments with Cdc7 inhibitor and flavopiridol.

claim: E2 treatment leads to a dramatic increase in RNA-DNA hybrids as detected by the S9.6 antibody.
source: We observed a dramatic increase in RNA-DNA hybrids upon E2 treatment (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by slot blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: RNase H treatment abolished the S9.6 signal, indicating antibody specificity for RNA-DNA hybrids.
source: Moreover, RNase H treatment, which specifically removes the RNA strand of an RNA-DNA hybrid, abolished the signal (Figure 2A), indicating antibody specificity for RNA-DNA hybrids.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by slot blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In mock-treated MCF7 cells, 17,445 DRIP peaks were observed across the genome.
source: In mock-treated MCF7 cells, we observed 17,445 DRIP peaks across the genome (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 1), a number in line with the previous DRIP-seq experiments performed in human Ntera2 cells and primary human fibroblasts (Ginno et al., 2012; Lim et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by DRIP-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In cells treated with E2 for 2 hr, 33,458 DRIP peaks were observed.
source: Strikingly, however, in cells treated with E2 we observed a dramatic increase in DRIP peaks, with 33,458 or 24,781 peaks at 2 or 24 hr, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 2, 3).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by DRIP-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In cells treated with E2 for 24 hr, 24,781 DRIP peaks were observed.
source: Strikingly, however, in cells treated with E2 we observed a dramatic increase in DRIP peaks, with 33,458 or 24,781 peaks at 2 or 24 hr, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 2, 3).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by DRIP-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: DRIP peaks from mock-treated cells covered 49.0 Mb of genome space.
source: DRIP peaks from mock-treated cells covered 49.0 Mb of genome space, while those from E2-treated cells for 2 hr or 24 hr covered 81.9 MB and 63.2 Mb of genome space, respectively.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and is derived from DRIP-seq data analysis.

claim: DRIP peaks from E2-treated cells for 2 hr covered 81.9 Mb of genome space.
source: DRIP peaks from mock-treated cells covered 49.0 Mb of genome space, while those from E2-treated cells for 2 hr or 24 hr covered 81.9 MB and 63.2 Mb of genome space, respectively.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and is derived from DRIP-seq data analysis.

claim: DRIP peaks from E2-treated cells for 24 hr covered 63.2 Mb of genome space.
source: DRIP peaks from mock-treated cells covered 49.0 Mb of genome space, while those from E2-treated cells for 2 hr or 24 hr covered 81.9 MB and 63.2 Mb of genome space, respectively.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and is derived from DRIP-seq data analysis.

claim: The vast majority of DRIP peaks were abolished by RNase H treatment.
source: Importantly, the vast majority of peaks were abolished by RNase H treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by DRIP-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: DRIP peaks were enriched at promoters, 5' gene regions and sites of transcriptional termination.
source: Indeed, DRIP peaks were enriched at promoters, 5' gene regions and sites of transcriptional termination (Figure 2B), consistent with their published distribution and roles at these regulatory regions (Ginno et al., 2013; Ginno et al., 2012; Skourti-Stathaki et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by meta-gene analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: DRIP peaks exhibited GC skew.
source: DRIP peaks also exhibited GC skew (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) and overlapped with in vitro mapped G-quartets (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) (Chambers et al., 2015), two sequence characteristics that are associated with R-loop formation (Duquette et al., 2004; Ginno et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by GC skew analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: DRIP peaks overlapped with in vitro mapped G-quartets.
source: DRIP peaks also exhibited GC skew (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) and overlapped with in vitro mapped G-quartets (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) (Chambers et al., 2015), two sequence characteristics that are associated with R-loop formation (Duquette et al., 2004; Ginno et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by G-quartet analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: GC skew and G-quartet formation are sequence characteristics associated with R-loop formation.
source: DRIP peaks also exhibited GC skew (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) and overlapped with in vitro mapped G-quartets (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) (Chambers et al., 2015), two sequence characteristics that are associated with R-loop formation (Duquette et al., 2004; Ginno et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: E2 treatment is associated with a dramatic induction of R-loops at new genomic sites.
source: Taken together, these observations suggest that E2 treatment is associated with a dramatic induction of R-loops at new genomic sites.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the DRIP-seq data showing increased DRIP peaks upon E2 treatment.

claim: 8,023 DRIP peaks were significantly induced at 2 hr of E2 treatment.
source: Analysis of RNA-DNA hybrids induced after E2 treatment revealed a dramatic increase throughout the genome, with 8,023 and 3,263 peaks significantly induced at 2 hr or 24 hr, respectively (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplements 1A,B, Figure 2C — source data 1, 2).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by differential DRIP peak analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 3,263 DRIP peaks were significantly induced at 24 hr of E2 treatment.
source: Analysis of RNA-DNA hybrids induced after E2 treatment revealed a dramatic increase throughout the genome, with 8,023 and 3,263 peaks significantly induced at 2 hr or 24 hr, respectively (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplements 1A,B, Figure 2C — source data 1, 2).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by differential DRIP peak analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Approximately 60% of RNA-DNA hybrids induced at 24 hr were also significantly induced at 2 hr.
source: Of those hybrids induced at 24 hr, ~60% were also significantly induced at 2 hr, suggesting that the E2 treatment can result in a sustained increase in R-loop formation at many loci.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and is derived from DRIP-seq data analysis.

claim: E2 treatment can result in a sustained increase in R-loop formation at many loci.
source: Of those hybrids induced at 24 hr, ~60% were also significantly induced at 2 hr, suggesting that the E2 treatment can result in a sustained increase in R-loop formation at many loci.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that many R-loops persist from 2 hr to 24 hr.

claim: XBP1 showed a robust increase in R-loops following E2 addition.
source: Loci that showed a robust increase following E2 addition include XBP1, CCND1 (Cyclin D1), and SLC7A5 (Figure 2D,E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), all targets of E2-transcription (Honkela et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by IGV display shown in Figure 2D.

claim: CCND1 (Cyclin D1) showed a robust increase in R-loops following E2 addition.
source: Loci that showed a robust increase following E2 addition include XBP1, CCND1 (Cyclin D1), and SLC7A5 (Figure 2D,E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), all targets of E2-transcription (Honkela et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by IGV display shown in Figure 2E.

claim: SLC7A5 showed a robust increase in R-loops following E2 addition.
source: Loci that showed a robust increase following E2 addition include XBP1, CCND1 (Cyclin D1), and SLC7A5 (Figure 2D,E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), all targets of E2-transcription (Honkela et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by IGV display shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: XBP1, CCND1, and SLC7A5 are all targets of E2-transcription.
source: Loci that showed a robust increase following E2 addition include XBP1, CCND1 (Cyclin D1), and SLC7A5 (Figure 2D,E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), all targets of E2-transcription (Honkela et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: A dose-dependent increase in DRIP signal was observed upon both 10 nM and 100 nM E2 treatment at several E2-transcription targets.
source: A dose-dependent increase in DRIP signal was observed upon both 10 nM and 100 nM E2 treatment at several E2-transcription targets (Figure 2F), while two genomic regions (MLKL and 83/84) devoid of DRIP peaks showed no change.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by DRIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Two genomic regions (MLKL and 83/84) devoid of DRIP peaks showed no change in DRIP signal upon E2 treatment.
source: A dose-dependent increase in DRIP signal was observed upon both 10 nM and 100 nM E2 treatment at several E2-transcription targets (Figure 2F), while two genomic regions (MLKL and 83/84) devoid of DRIP peaks showed no change.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by DRIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: E2-induced RNA-DNA hybrids are dramatically enriched in E2-transcriptionally responsive genes at both 2 hr and 24 hr time points.
source: We found a dramatic enrichment of R-loops in E2-transcriptionally responsive genes at both time points (Figure 2G, red highlighting).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by GREAT analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The induction of R-loops by E2 is a robust response that occurs quickly at E2-responsive genes, and persists at a subset of these genes.
source: These data clearly demonstrate that the induction of R-loops by E2 is a robust response that occurs quickly at E2-responsive genes, and persists at a subset of these genes.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the DRIP-seq and GREAT analysis data.

claim: R-loop formation occurs prior to the onset of DNA damage.
source: Taken together with data shown in Figure 1, these data also demonstrate that R-loop formation occurs prior to the onset of DNA damage, and in cells that have not yet entered S phase (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that R-loops are induced at 2 hr while DNA damage is not significant until later time points.

claim: R-loop formation occurs in cells that have not yet entered S phase.
source: Taken together with data shown in Figure 1, these data also demonstrate that R-loop formation occurs prior to the onset of DNA damage, and in cells that have not yet entered S phase (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by FACS data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: A modest correlation between the induction of DRIP signal and the induction of expression was observed.
source: A modest correlation between the induction of DRIP signal and the induction of expression was observed, consistent with the requirement for transcription in R-loop formation.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and is derived from correlation analysis with GRO-seq data.

claim: The majority of induced DRIP peaks were found in E2-responsive genes.
source: Although the majority of induced DRIP peaks were found in E2-responsive genes (red highlighting), some were also induced at sites that were not E2-responsive or that were negatively regulated by E2 (blue highlighting).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Some induced DRIP peaks were also induced at sites that were not E2-responsive or that were negatively regulated by E2.
source: Although the majority of induced DRIP peaks were found in E2-responsive genes (red highlighting), some were also induced at sites that were not E2-responsive or that were negatively regulated by E2 (blue highlighting).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2H.

claim: DRIP peaks do not form only on highly expressed genes.
source: We also found no meaningful correlation between DRIP signal enrichment and overall expression level as measured by publically available RNA-seq data from similarly paired conditions. This finding indicates that DRIP peaks do not form only on highly expressed genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: R-loop induction by E2 is correlated with E2-induced transcription, but expression level is not the sole determinant of R-loop formation.
source: We conclude that R-loop induction by E2 is correlated with E2-induced transcription, but that expression level is not the sole determinant of R-loop formation and other secondary structures or sequence elements may contribute.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the correlation analyses with GRO-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: Other secondary structures or sequence elements may contribute to R-loop formation.
source: We conclude that R-loop induction by E2 is correlated with E2-induced transcription, but that expression level is not the sole determinant of R-loop formation and other secondary structures or sequence elements may contribute.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observation that expression level alone does not fully explain R-loop formation.

claim: Structural variants in breast cancer are significantly enriched in genes that are transcriptionally-responsive to E2.
source: Notably, we observed a significant enrichment of both structural variants (p<1.00*10−6) and translocations (p<1.00*10−6) in genes that are transcriptionally-responsive to E2 (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Translocations in breast cancer are significantly enriched in genes that are transcriptionally-responsive to E2.
source: Notably, we observed a significant enrichment of both structural variants (p<1.00*10−6) and translocations (p<1.00*10−6) in genes that are transcriptionally-responsive to E2 (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There were fewer simple somatic mutations in E2-responsive loci relative to the matched set.
source: In contrast, there were fewer simple somatic mutations in E2-responsive loci relative to the matched set (p<1.00*10−6) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Genes whose expression is induced in response to E2 are enriched in genomic rearrangements in breast tumors.
source: These results demonstrate that genes whose expression is induced in response to E2 are enriched in genomic rearrangements in breast tumors and support the view that these sites are prone to certain types of DNA damage.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the enrichment analysis of breast cancer mutations.

claim: E2-responsive sites are prone to certain types of DNA damage.
source: These results demonstrate that genes whose expression is induced in response to E2 are enriched in genomic rearrangements in breast tumors and support the view that these sites are prone to certain types of DNA damage.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the enrichment of rearrangements in E2-responsive genes.

claim: The percentage of cells that contain at least one PLA focus in the nucleus increased approximately 2-fold following E2 treatment.
source: Notably, the percentage of cells that contain at least one PLA focus in the nucleus increased approximately 2-fold following E2 treatment (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by PLA data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: The majority of DNA damage may occur at a distance from the R-loop that is outside the limits of PLA detection (<30–40 nM).
source: The relatively small number of detectable interactions between the RNA-DNA hybrid and P-H2AX antibodies upon E2 addition may indicate that the majority of DNA damage occurs at a distance from the R-loop that is outside the limits of PLA detection (<30–40 nM).
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observation of relatively few PLA foci.

claim: Both P-H2AX and P-KAP1 interacted with RNA-DNA hybrid containing chromatin fragments.
source: We found that that both P-H2AX and another DDR target, P-KAP1, interacted with RNA-DNA hybrid containing chromatin fragments (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The interaction between P-H2AX/P-KAP1 and RNA-DNA hybrids was specific, as it did not occur with MCM3.
source: This interaction was specific, as it did not occur with MCM3, another chromatin-bound protein (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: DNA damage markers bind the chromatin environment near R-loops following E2 treatment.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that DNA damage markers bind the chromatin environment near R-loops following E2 treatment.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the PLA and co-IP experiments.

claim: Expression of RNase H resulted in a dramatic and dose-dependent reduction in P-H2AX intensity and foci formation upon E2 treatment.
source: Strikingly, we observed a dramatic and dose-dependent reduction in P-H2AX intensity and foci formation upon increasing RNase H expression (Figure 4E,F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: Expression of RNase H did not alter E2-driven cell cycle progression.
source: Importantly, expression of RNase H did not alter E2-driven cell cycle progression (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), nor did it reduce global levels of transcription, as measured by EU labeling (Figure 4—figure supplements 4A,B).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by FACS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Expression of RNase H did not reduce global levels of transcription, as measured by EU labeling.
source: Importantly, expression of RNase H did not alter E2-driven cell cycle progression (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), nor did it reduce global levels of transcription, as measured by EU labeling (Figure 4—figure supplements 4A,B).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by EU staining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 4A,B.

claim: The decreased P-H2AX signal upon RNase H expression is not a result of reduced transcription or a defect in cell cycle progression.
source: Thus, the decreased P-H2AX signal is not a result of reduced transcription or a defect in cell cycle progression.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observations that RNase H does not affect transcription or cell cycle.

claim: RNase H expression resulted in a significant decrease in DSBs upon E2 stimulation, as measured by the neutral comet assay.
source: Finally, we found that RNase H expression resulted in a significant decrease in DSBs upon E2 stimulation, as measured by the neutral comet assay (Figure 4G,H).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by neutral comet assay data shown in Figure 4G,H.

claim: RNA-DNA hybrids are needed to form E2-induced DSBs.
source: These findings clearly demonstrate that RNA-DNA hybrids are needed to form E2-induced DSBs.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the RNase H overexpression experiments.

claim: R-loop-mediated DSB formation depends on factors specifically involved in transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair (TC-NER), but not factors specifically involved in global genome NER (GG-NER).
source: We recently showed that R-loop-mediated DSB formation depends on factors specifically involved in transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair (TC-NER), but not factors specifically involved in global genome NER (GG-NER) (Sollier et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: P-H2AX levels were significantly reduced following knockdown of XPG.
source: Strikingly, we found that P-H2AX levels were significantly reduced following knockdown of XPG, an endonuclease involved in both forms NER (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: XPG knockdown dramatically reduced the comet tail moment that forms in response to E2 treatment.
source: XPG knockdown also dramatically reduced the comet tail moment that forms in response to E2 treatment (Figure 5B,C), signifying a significant reduction in E2-mediated DSBs.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by neutral comet assay data shown in Figure 5B,C.

claim: Knockdown of the TC-NER specific factor Cockayne syndrome group B (CSB) significantly reduced P-H2AX levels induced by E2.
source: Importantly, we also found that knockdown of the TC-NER specific factor Cockayne syndrome group B (CSB) significantly reduced P-H2AX levels induced by E2 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Knockdown of XPC, a lesion-recognition factor specifically involved in GG-NER, caused little change in P-H2AX levels after E2 treatment.
source: In contrast, knockdown of XPC, a lesion-recognition factor specifically involved in GG-NER, caused little change in P-H2AX levels after E2 treatment (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: R-loops induced by E2 are processed by TC-NER factors.
source: These findings suggest that R-loops induced by E2 are processed by TC-NER factors.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential effects of TC-NER and GG-NER factor knockdowns.

claim: Replication-dependent E2-induced DNA damage results from the induction of R-loops triggered by E2-mediated transcription.
source: Taken as a whole, our findings demonstrate that replication-dependent E2-induced DNA damage results from the induction of R-loops triggered by E2-mediated transcription.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from all the experimental data presented.

claim: TopoIIβ and APOBEC3B cause the rapid and transient formation of DNA damage in a process necessary for E2-induced transcriptional activation.
source: For example, TopoIIβ and APOBEC3B cause the rapid and transient formation of DNA damage in a process necessary for E2-induced transcriptional activation (Ju et al., 2006; Periyasamy et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: E2 metabolites can cause oxidative DNA damage.
source: Additionally, E2 metabolites can cause oxidative DNA damage (Lavigne et al., 2001; Yager, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Although E2 causes a dramatic increase in R-loops after 2 hr, no significant change in DNA damage is observed at that time.
source: Although E2 causes a dramatic increase in R-loops after 2 hr (Figure 2C), no significant change in DNA damage is observed at that time (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figures 1F and 2C.

claim: R-loops are present but do not cause DNA damage until S phase entry.
source: Thus, although R-loops are present, they do not cause DNA damage until S phase entry.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that R-loops form before DNA damage and that DNA damage requires replication.

claim: R-loop-dependent DNA damage has been previously associated with DNA replication.
source: Consistent with this finding, R-loop-dependent DNA damage has been previously associated with DNA replication (Alzu et al., 2012; Gan et al., 2011; Houlard et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A few common fragile sites correspond to late-replicating, long genes where R-loops form.
source: Moreover, a few common fragile sites correspond to late-replicating, long genes where R-loops form, and early-replicating fragile sites are associated with highly transcribed genes (Barlow et al., 2013; Helmrich et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Early-replicating fragile sites are associated with highly transcribed genes.
source: Moreover, a few common fragile sites correspond to late-replicating, long genes where R-loops form, and early-replicating fragile sites are associated with highly transcribed genes (Barlow et al., 2013; Helmrich et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Genes that are highly transcribed or R-loop prone may pose the greatest challenge to genome integrity when they meet the replication fork.
source: This suggests that genes that are highly transcribed or R-loop prone may pose the greatest challenge to genome integrity when they meet the replication fork.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the association of fragile sites with transcription and R-loops.

claim: TC-NER factors may be acting in a non-canonical manner in S phase.
source: This raises the possibility that these factors may be acting in a non-canonical manner in S phase, and there are several possible mechanisms by which their activity may be coordinated with replication activities that have been previously discussed (see Sollier et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observation that TC-NER factors are involved in replication-dependent damage.

claim: R-loops are induced predominantly at E2-responsive genes (p<10−233).
source: Importantly, we find that R-loops are induced predominantly at E2-responsive genes (p<10−233).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and is derived from GREAT analysis.

claim: A small subset of genomic regions exist that show a significant increase in R-loops despite no increase in expression.
source: Interestingly, a small subset of genomic regions exist that show a significant increase in R-loops despite no increase in expression (Figure 2H, blue highlighting).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2H.

claim: RPL13A, the expression of which is unaffected by E2, showed a significant increase in R-loops upon E2.
source: Similarly, RPL13A, the expression of which is unaffected by E2 (Shah and Faridi, 2011), showed a significant increase in R-loops upon E2 (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by DRIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Upon a burst in transcription, the cell's normal splicing and R-loop modulating factors initially become saturated.
source: One possibility is that upon a burst in transcription, the cell's normal splicing and R-loop modulating factors initially become saturated.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposed as a possible explanation for R-loop formation at non-responsive genes.

claim: Some loci that are prone to form R-loops may accumulate these structures and become vulnerable to DNA damage, regardless of their response to the transcription stimulus.
source: Thus, some loci that are prone to form R-loops may accumulate these structures and become vulnerable to DNA damage, regardless of their response to the transcription stimulus.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposed as a possible explanation for R-loop formation at non-responsive genes.

claim: Both structural variants and translocations have been suggested to occur due to erroneous repair of a DSB.
source: Both structural variants and translocations have been suggested to occur due to erroneous repair of a DSB (Kasparek and Humphrey, 2011) and these mutation types have been shown to be more prevalent in breast tumors relative to other tumor tissues (Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Structural variants and translocations have been shown to be more prevalent in breast tumors relative to other tumor tissues.
source: Both structural variants and translocations have been suggested to occur due to erroneous repair of a DSB (Kasparek and Humphrey, 2011) and these mutation types have been shown to be more prevalent in breast tumors relative to other tumor tissues (Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: E2 induces robust R-loop formation at Cyclin D1.
source: For example, we observed a dramatic increase in R-loops at Cyclin D1 (Figure 2E), which is amplified in up to 20% of breast cancers, the majority of which are ER-positive (Arnold and Papanikolaou, 2005; Osborne et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by IGV display shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Cyclin D1 is amplified in up to 20% of breast cancers, the majority of which are ER-positive.
source: For example, we observed a dramatic increase in R-loops at Cyclin D1 (Figure 2E), which is amplified in up to 20% of breast cancers, the majority of which are ER-positive (Arnold and Papanikolaou, 2005; Osborne et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: E2 induces robust R-loop formation at ZNF703.
source: Similarly, E2 induces robust R-loop formation at ZNF703.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: ZNF703 has been implicated in driving oncogenesis in luminal B breast tumors.
source: This locus has been implicated in driving oncogenesis in luminal B breast tumors (Holland et al., 2011; Sircoulomb et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Both Cyclin D1 and ZNF703 were among the genes identified as breast cancer drivers.
source: Both Cyclin D1 and ZNF703 were among the genes identified as breast cancer drivers, as were an additional 27 genes with E2-induced R-loops (Nik-Zainal et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: An additional 27 genes with E2-induced R-loops were identified as breast cancer drivers.
source: Both Cyclin D1 and ZNF703 were among the genes identified as breast cancer drivers, as were an additional 27 genes with E2-induced R-loops (Nik-Zainal et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: E2-induced R-loop formation could lead to DNA damage and genome instability at some R-loop prone loci.
source: Our findings raise the possibility that E2-induced R-loop formation could lead to DNA damage and genome instability at some of these and other R-loop prone loci.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the findings of R-loops at cancer driver genes.

claim: Testosterone (DHT) stimulation in prostate cells has been shown to lead to DSBs and recurrent translocations at androgen-receptor (AR) target loci.
source: Intriguingly, testosterone (DHT) stimulation in prostate cells has been shown to lead to DSBs and recurrent translocations at androgen-receptor (AR) target loci (Haffner et al., 2010; Lin et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: DHT-induced breaks are TOP2B-dependent and necessary for the induction of transcription.
source: While these breaks are TOP2B-dependent and necessary for the induction of transcription, DHT may also induce DNA damage in an R-loop and replication dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: DHT may also induce DNA damage in an R-loop and replication dependent manner.
source: While these breaks are TOP2B-dependent and necessary for the induction of transcription, DHT may also induce DNA damage in an R-loop and replication dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is speculative, drawing a parallel to the E2 findings.

claim: In prostate cancer, recurrent rearrangements are frequently observed at androgen-receptor (AR) target genes.
source: Notably, in prostate cancer, recurrent rearrangements are frequently observed at androgen-receptor (AR) target genes (Kumar-Sinha et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The induction of potentially toxic R-loops at sites of induced transcription may offer insight into the tissue-specific DNA damage and mutation patterns observed in some cancers.
source: Thus, the induction of potentially toxic R-loops at sites of induced transcription may offer insight into the tissue-specific DNA damage and mutation patterns observed in some cancers.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a broader implication of the findings.
